introduction_markdown: Multiple choice paper (0730 English Language 1, GCE Advanced Level, June 2026). Duration: one and a half hours. Answer ALL the 50 questions; all questions carry equal marks. Each question has four suggested answers A, B, C and D: choose the one that best answers the question and mark it on the answer sheet with a soft HB pencil (one answer only; more than one mark scores zero for that question). Avoid spending too much time on any one question. Mobile phones are not allowed in the examination room. The paper has four sections: A reading comprehension (questions 1-10, 10 marks), B speech work (questions 11-20, 10 marks), C grammar (questions 21-40, 20 marks) and D vocabulary (questions 41-50, 10 marks).
enonce_intro_markdown: **Multiple choice questions** - choose the one best answer, A, B, C or D.
incertitudes: Sujet de 6 pages (page de garde : ADVANCED LEVEL, 0730 English Language 1, JUNE 2026, QCM d'une heure et demie, 50 questions de points egaux), scan sans couche texte avec filigrane : chaque page a ete relue en image, puis recontrolee a fort grossissement. Les sections imprimees sont A reading comprehension (questions 1-10, 10 points), B speech work (11-20, 10 points), C grammar (21-40, 20 points) et D vocabulary (41-50, 10 points), soit 50 ; les points sont ceux du sujet, non modifies.
Aucun corrige ni aucune cle n'est fourni : toutes les cles sont etablies par raisonnement sur le passage et sur les regles de langue (grammaire, phonetique, vocabulaire).

Passage de comprehension (lignes 1 a 66) recopie en entier avec les numeros de ligne imprimes (tous les cinq), fautes imprimees comprises : 'justices and equality' (ligne 14), 'social challenge' (ligne 46, pour social change), 'hatred and justice' (ligne 64), 'Basic human rights are under constant threats' (ligne 10), 'justice-that' (ligne 62). Le sigle de l'association est imprime avec des variantes (ISCC - JPBDA, ISCC-JPBDA, ISCC_ JPBDA, ISCC _ JPBDA) : il est transcrit 'ISCC - JPBDA' et 'ISCC-JPBDA' quand le tiret est lisible, 'ISCC_JPBDA' sinon (blanc ou trait de soulignement indeterminable sur le scan). Les tirets longs imprimes sont rendus par un tiret simple. Le passage est un texte promotionnel tire d'un site web (source citee : lausanne.org).

Defauts d'impression conserves : Q12 'syllabus' pour 'syllables' ; Q13 options A et B identiques a un espace pres ('ex-tra-or-di-na-ry') ; Q16 phrase 'My sister bought fruits vegetable and meat' sans virgules (la coupure avant 'meat' est un retour a la ligne de la page) ; Q23 option C imprimee 'hadn't been earing' (faute pour 'eating', transcrite 'eating') ; Q29 'it just' apres le premier blanc ; Q39 options A et D identiques ; Q50 mot 'stellar' souligne, Q49 mot 'imbued' souligne (rendus en gras).

Questions converties en questions OUVERTES (aucune lettre n'est choisie au hasard) : Q6 (aucune option ne reprend la liste des parties prenantes des lignes 35-37, B est la plus proche) ; Q17 (aisle, bright et, par la lettre muette finale, kite contiennent une lettre muette) ; Q18 (aucune des quatre paires n'a la meme voyelle : lead, tear, read et bass changent de voyelle ; le sujet voulait sans doute 'different') ; Q25 (plenty of, lots of et a lot of sont tous trois corrects devant milk) ; Q29 (A et C sont tous deux corrects : 'after I had finished' ou 'after I finished') ; Q34 (one another et each other sont tous deux acceptables, each other preferee pour deux personnes) ; Q39 (les options A et D sont imprimees a l'identique) ; Q48 (les ensembles B et D contiennent chacun un intrus : coward, bureaucracy).

Cles conservees mais a relire par un enseignant : Q5 (C, 'by highlighting stories of resilience and hope', alors que B 'shaping public opinion' est aussi mentionne a la ligne 45) ; Q7 (B armoury ; A weapons est defendable pour 'arsenal') ; Q8 (persuasive retenue contre argumentative) ; Q13 (C, cinq syllabes) ; Q16 (A, rise-fall des enumerations) ; Q20 (18 syllabes en comptant 'lions' pour deux) ; Q23 (A hadn't eaten) ; Q27 (D wonder if I could, C wondered if I could reste possible) ; Q42 (D freeze, le mot attendu ban n'est pas propose, B taboo concevable) ; Q45 (A unscientific) ; Q50 (D boring : l'antonyme mediocre n'est pas propose).
Aucune figure : le sujet ne contient ni image ni schema. Questions de phonetique (Q11-Q20) : les transcriptions API des corriges suivent la prononciation britannique standard.

Converties en questions ouvertes par le relecteur (clé ou options discutables) : 6, 17, 18, 25, 29, 34, 39, 48. Q6 : aucune option ne reprend la liste des lignes 35-37 ; Q17 : plusieurs mots ont une lettre muette ; Q18 : aucune paire n'a la meme voyelle ; Q25 : trois options correctes ; Q29 et Q34 : deux options acceptables ; Q39 : options A et D identiques ; Q48 : deux ensembles contiennent un intrus.

Seconde passe faite : les 6 pages ont ete relues en image a fort grossissement (passage compare ligne a ligne, options comparees une a une) et les 50 questions ont ete refaites une deuxieme fois independamment ; aucune cle n'a change.

questions.enonce_markdown:
**SECTION A: READING COMPREHENSION (10 marks).** Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions that follow it. Choose the best answer for each question from the alternatives A, B, C and D.

**Passage for questions 1 to 10** (line numbers are printed in square brackets, every fifth line)

At a time when our world seems increasingly fractured by conflict, injustice, and moral decay, it is essential for
communities to engage in deep reflection on the fundamental values of peace, justice, and human dignity. The Ideal
Solutions for Community Communication - Justice, Peace Building and Development Association (ISCC - JPBDA)
stands as a beacon of hope amid this pervasive brokenness witnessed nowadays. This organization, (ISCC\_JPBDA) is
dedicated to fostering an environment where dialogue, understanding, and collaboration can flourish,  [5]
enabling communities to heal and rebuild themselves.

The reality of a broken world reveals that, from local neighbourhoods to the global stage, the forces of hatred,
inequality, and violence continue to erode the very foundations of human existence. In many regions, communities find
themselves trapped in cycles of mistrust, betrayal and division, exacerbated by economic disparities and social injustice
created by man. Basic human rights are under constant threats, with marginalised groups, often suffering  [10]
the most. Reports of violence and discrimination flood the media, creating an atmosphere of fear and hopelessness
among affected communities. The impacts of these issues are felt widely, as they ripple through families,
neighbourhoods, and entire societies. Children grow up in environments marked by tension and strife, and the future
looks bleak when the fundamental principles of justices and equality are disregarded.

In the face of these overwhelming challenges, ISCC-JPBDA reaffirms its unwavering mission, which is to  [15]
combat the forces that divide us. Its commitment is rooted in three core objectives which are: fighting hate speech,
racism, and tribalism, advocating for justice, equity, and human dignity and empowering communities through
innovation and collaboration.

Hate speech and discrimination have become alarmingly prevalent in today's society, often fuelled by misinformation
and fear. It believes in promoting social cohesion and dialogue as crucial means of countering these destructive  [20]
forces that loom among us. By fostering conversations among diverse groups, it aims to build bridges of understanding
and empathy, breaking down barriers that separate us.

Every individual deserves to live in a society where his or her rights are respected and upheld. Ideal Solution for
Community Communication, Justice, Peace Building and Development Association (ISCC\_JPBDA) advocacy efforts
focus on ensuring that justice systems are fair and equitable, addressing systemic inequalities that plague  [25]
many communities. It strives to amplify the voices of those who have been marginalised; working to create a world
where human dignity is a priority for all.

It believes that sustainable solutions arise when communities are empowered to take ownership of their challenges. By
promoting innovation and collaboration, ISCC\_JPBDA encourages individuals and groups to develop practical
solutions, tailored to their unique circumstances. Its initiatives focus on equipping communities with the  [30]
tools and resources necessary for meaningful change.

In a world that feels fragmented and hopeless, it holds firm to the belief that it is possible to mend the fabrics of society
when individuals unite around shared values. Its vision is rooted in the conviction that it is never too late to do the right
thing, to stand up for what is just, and to work towards a brighter future.

Ideal Solution for Community Communication, Justice, Peace Building and Development Association  [35]
(ISCC\_JPBDA) calls upon all stakeholders - government bodies, civil society organisations, faith leaders, and
community members - to join in the vital work of rebuilding a society that upholds justice, peace, and unity. Together,
we can create a powerful movement that fosters healing and reconciliation, transforming our broken world into one that
thrives on mutual respect and understanding.

One of the most effective tools in its arsenal is education. By raising awareness about the issues that plague  [40]
our communities, we can empower individuals to take action. Educational initiatives can inspire people to challenge
harmful stereotypes and misconceptions while promoting a culture of acceptance and understanding. Workshops,
seminars, and community programmes can play pivotal roles in this effort, providing platforms for dialogue and
learning.

Moreover, the role of media cannot be understated. Responsible journalism has the power to shape public opinion  [45]
and drive social challenge. By highlighting stories of resilience and hope, the media can counterbalance the negativity
that often dominates headlines. ISCC\_JPBDA encourages media outlets to focus on constructive narratives that
celebrate diversity and promote unity.

Building resilience in communities is non-negotiable. To address the challenges of a broken world, we must also focus
on building resilience within communities. This involves creating supportive networks that empower individuals  [50]
to overcome adversity. Programmes that foster mental health and well-being are critical, as they equip individuals with
the coping mechanisms necessary to navigate life's challenges.

Additionally, fostering economic opportunities is essential for community resilience. By supporting global business
and promoting entrepreneurship, we can help communities thrive economically, reducing dependence on external aid
and fostering a sense of ownership and pride.  [55]

In this broken world, every act of kindness, every voice raised for truth, and every effort to protect the vulnerable is a
step towards healing. Together, we can transform division into unity and despair into hope. The path ahead may be
fraught with challenges, but with steadfast determination and collective action, we can create a future characterised by
justice, peace, and shared humanity.

Ideal Solution for Community Communication, Justice, Peace Building and Development Association  [60]
(ISCC\_JPBDA) firmly believes that the seeds of change lie within each of us. It is through our combined efforts -
grounded in compassion and a commitment to justice-that we can mend the fractures in our world, building hope and
justice for all. Through these efforts, we can give a chance to everyone to feel loved, and cared for, thereby reducing
the cycle of discrimination, hatred and justice. The Ideal Solution for Community Communication, Justice, Peace
Building and Development Association (ISCC\_JPBDA) believes that an ideal world that fosters  [65]
justice, peace-building and development is possible if the broken walls are rebuilt.

Source: Culled from the internet: https://www.lausanne.org

1. The fundamental values that can heal and rebuild a broken world are \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Lines 1-2 say that communities must reflect on "the fundamental values of peace, justice, and human dignity", and these are the values on which the broken world is to be rebuilt. A names the conditions that help communities heal (dialogue, understanding and collaboration, line 5), not the values themselves. B and D mix the fields of work and the name of the association (ISCC-JPBDA).

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Passage for questions 1 to 10 above)

2. A broken world is characterised by \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The passage describes the broken world through inequality (line 8), betrayal (line 9) and hopelessness (line 11), so B is the only option whose three items are all found there. A and D contain *equality*, which is the opposite of what characterises a broken world (line 14 says that the principles of justice and equality are disregarded). C contains *human rights*, which the passage says are under constant threat (line 10), not a feature of the broken world.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Passage for questions 1 to 10 above)

3. ISCC-JPBDA has as its core mission to \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Lines 15-16: ISCC-JPBDA "reaffirms its unwavering mission, which is to combat the forces that divide us". The other options come after this statement and are objectives or means: fighting hate speech, racism and tribalism and empowering communities (lines 16-18), and promoting social cohesion and dialogue (lines 20-21). The question asks for the core mission, which is the general one stated in lines 15-16.

**Answer: A.**

choix.texte: combat the forces that divide communities
empower communities through innovation and cohesion
counter hate speech, racism, and tribalism

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Passage for questions 1 to 10 above)

4. According to the passage, the term *'advocacy'* means \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Lines 23-27: the association's "advocacy efforts focus on ensuring that justice systems are fair and equitable, addressing systemic inequalities" and amplifying "the voices of those who have been marginalised". To advocate is to speak publicly in support of a cause, here the cause of the marginalised, so A is correct. B is a belief stated in line 28, C is the opposite of the sense (the association fights for justice), and D is the general aim of the whole mission, not the meaning of the word.

**Answer: A.**
themes: A Level English - vocabulary in context

choix.texte: pleading the cause of the marginalised
believing that sustainable solutions can arise

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Passage for questions 1 to 10 above)

5. The passage suggests that the media can contribute positively to society by \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Lines 46-47: "By highlighting stories of resilience and hope, the media can counterbalance the negativity that often dominates headlines". The sentence has exactly the form of the question (by + ing), so C is the positive contribution named by the passage. B (line 45-46: responsible journalism "has the power to shape public opinion") states a power, which is positive only if the journalism is responsible and constructive; A is not mentioned for the media, and D is the opposite of what the passage asks (lines 41-42 say that education challenges stereotypes and misconceptions).

**Answer: C.**

choix.texte: highlighting stories of resilience and hope

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Passage for questions 1 to 10 above)

6. Major stakeholders in rebuilding broken communities are \_\_\_\_\_\_.

*Options as printed:* A) ISCC-JPBDA   B) the media, associations, and educationists   C) vulnerable children   D) entrepreneurs and the voiceless
questions.corrige_markdown:
Lines 35-37: ISCC-JPBDA "calls upon all stakeholders - government bodies, civil society organisations, faith leaders, and community members". None of the four printed options repeats this list. A is the association that makes the call, C and D name beneficiaries (vulnerable children, the voiceless) or one economic group (entrepreneurs, lines 53-54), not stakeholders called to join the work. B is the closest: associations correspond to civil society organisations, and the media (lines 44-48) and education (lines 40-44) are named as agents of change.

**Intended answer: B (the media, associations, and educationists), the closest of the four printed options.**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Passage for questions 1 to 10 above)

7. *'One of the most effective tools in the arsenal of ISCC-JPBDA is education.'* The word **'arsenal'** as used in the passage (L.40) means \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
An *arsenal* is a place where weapons are made or kept, and by extension the whole range of means that someone has at their disposal. In line 40, "tools in its arsenal" means the tools in its armoury, that is, the resources the organisation can use. B is the nearest word (armoury: a store or collection of weapons, and figuratively of resources). A (weapons) names the items themselves, and "tools in its weapons" would not make sense; C and D name ordinary storage places without the idea of means or weapons.

**Answer: B.**
themes: A Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Passage for questions 1 to 10 above)

8. This passage is best described as \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The writer's purpose is to win the reader's support for ISCC-JPBDA and to move readers to act: the text calls upon all stakeholders "to join in the vital work" (lines 35-37), uses emotive language ("broken world", "hope", "healing") and repeated appeals ("Together, we can...", lines 37-38 and 57). A descriptive text would only describe; an expository text would explain neutrally; an argumentative text would defend a thesis with evidence against opposing views, which the passage does not do. The passage is therefore persuasive.

**Answer: B.**
themes: A Level English - text types and purpose

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Passage for questions 1 to 10 above)

9. The overall theme of the passage is \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
From the first paragraph to the last, the passage speaks of a world torn by injustice and hatred and of the hope that justice, peace and shared humanity can mend it. The media (A) are only one tool, discussed in one paragraph (lines 45-48); the association (B) is the speaker, but the passage describes its mission and beliefs, not its exploits (achievements); C is contradicted by the stress on communities taking ownership of their own challenges (lines 28-29).

**Answer: D.**

choix.texte: The role of the media in peace building
The role of external forces in bringing change
Hope and justice for a broken world

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Passage for questions 1 to 10 above)

10. A suitable title for this passage could be \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
A good title covers the whole text. The passage describes a broken world (paragraphs 1-2), the mission and means of the association, and ends on the hope that the world can be rebuilt ("if the broken walls are rebuilt", line 66). A covers all of this. B, C and D each cover only one part (the mission, one of its objectives, one of its aims).

**Answer: A.**

choix.texte: Rebuilding life in a Broken World

questions.enonce_markdown:
**SECTION B: SPEECH WORK (10 marks).** Choose the alternative A, B, C or D that best completes each sentence below.

11. The word with the odd vowel sound is \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
*Heat* /hiːt/, *seat* /siːt/ and *meet* /miːt/ all have the long vowel /iː/. *Bit* /bɪt/ has the short vowel /ɪ/, so it is the odd one out.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 12. The word *'diabetes'* has \_\_\_\_\_\_ syllabus.
questions.corrige_markdown:
*Diabetes* is pronounced /ˌdaɪ.əˈbiː.tiːz/ (or /ˌdaɪ.əˈbiː.tɪs/): di-a-be-tes, four syllables. (The printed question says *syllabus* for *syllables*.)

**Answer: B.**
themes: A Level English - syllables and syllabification

questions.enonce_markdown: 13. The correct syllabification of the word *'extraordinary'* is \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
In normal speech *extraordinary* /ɪkˈstrɔː.dɪ.nə.ri/ has five syllables: ex-traor-di-na-ry, with the *-traor-* sequence said as one syllable /strɔː/. C gives this division. A and B (identical except for a stray space) split *-tra-or-* into two syllables and give six, which only reflects the rare pronunciation of the word as *extra + ordinary*; D divides *-nary* wrongly (din-a-ry).

**Answer: C.**
themes: A Level English - syllables and syllabification

questions.enonce_markdown: 14. *'Individual'* is best pronounced as \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
*Individual* /ˌɪn.dɪˈvɪdʒ.u.əl/ has five syllables (in-di-vi-du-al), with the main stress on the third syllable, VI. D marks the stress on that syllable. A puts it on the last syllable, B on the first and C on the second, and C also reduces the word to four syllables.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 15. The stress on the word *discrimination* falls on the \_\_\_\_\_\_ syllable.
questions.corrige_markdown:
*Discrimination* is divided dis-crim-i-na-tion (five syllables). Words ending in *-ation* carry the main stress on the syllable just before the ending: dis-crim-i-NA-tion, so the stress falls on the 4th syllable.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 16. The sentence which has a rise-fall intonation is \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
In a list, the voice rises on each item and falls on the last one (rise, rise, then fall): the sentence about fruits, vegetables and meat has this rise-fall pattern. B is a yes/no question and takes a rising tone; C is a plain statement and takes a falling tone; D is a statement followed by a tag, which takes a fall-rise or a rise. (The printed sentence in A has no commas and the break before *meat* is a line break of the printed page.)

**Answer: A.**

choix.texte: My sister bought fruits vegetable and meat

questions.enonce_markdown:
17. The word that contains a silent letter is \_\_\_\_\_\_.

*Options as printed:* A) aisle   B) kite   C) plant   D) bright
questions.corrige_markdown:
A silent letter is a letter that is written but not pronounced. *Aisle* /aɪl/ has a silent *s*; *bright* /braɪt/ has a silent *gh* (g and h are not pronounced); *kite* has a silent final *e* (it only shows that the *i* is long); in *plant* every letter is sounded. More than one printed option therefore qualifies (aisle and bright, and kite if the silent *e* is counted), so the question has no single safe key.

**Intended answer: A (aisle, silent s) or D (bright, silent gh); kite also has a silent final e.**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
18. The pair that has the same vowel sound is \_\_\_\_\_\_.

*Options as printed:* A) 'Lead' (to guide) - 'Lead' (a metal)   B) 'Tear' (to rip) - 'Tear' (a drop of liquid)   C) 'Read' (present) - 'Read' (past)   D) 'Bass' (a fish) - 'Bass' (low frequency sound)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Each pair is made of two words with the same spelling and different meanings (heteronyms), and in every pair the vowel sound changes: *lead* /liːd/ (to guide) and /led/ (the metal); *tear* /teə/ (to rip) and /tɪə/ (a drop); *read* /riːd/ (present) and /red/ (past); *bass* /bæs/ (the fish) and /beɪs/ (low sound). So no printed pair has the same vowel sound; the question probably meant *different* vowel sounds (or *same spelling*).

**Intended answer: none of the four printed pairs (the vowel sound changes in each pair).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: 19. \_\_\_\_\_\_ contains a long vowel sound.
questions.corrige_markdown:
*Sea* /siː/ has the long vowel /iː/. *Cup* /kʌp/, *dog* /dɒg/ and *bed* /bed/ have short vowels.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 20. *'The indomitable lions performed poorly during the tournament'*. This sentence has \_\_\_\_\_\_ syllables.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Count word by word: The (1) + in-dom-i-ta-ble (5) + li-ons (2) + per-formed (2) + poor-ly (2) + dur-ing (2) + the (1) + tour-na-ment (3) = 18 syllables. (*Lions* is /ˈlaɪ.ənz/, two syllables; counting it as one would give 17.)

**Answer: C.**
themes: A Level English - syllables and syllabification

questions.enonce_markdown:
**SECTION C: GRAMMAR (20 marks).** Choose the alternative A, B, C, or D that best completes each sentence below.

21. Had they known, they \_\_\_\_\_\_ published the right results.
questions.corrige_markdown:
*Had they known* is the inverted form of *If they had known*, a third conditional (unreal past). The main clause takes *would have* + past participle: they would have published the right results. *Would* alone, *will have* and *shall have* do not express an unreal past.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 22. By the end of 2027, the President \_\_\_\_\_\_ Cameroon for 45 years.
questions.corrige_markdown:
*By the end of 2027* points to a future time before or at which a period will be complete, so the future perfect is needed: will have ruled. *Would have ruled* is a past unreal form, *will be ruling* does not express completion by a date, and *would rule* is a conditional.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 23. I \_\_\_\_\_\_ all day yesterday, so I was hungry when I \_\_\_\_\_\_ home.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The lack of food happened before the moment in the past (getting home), so the first verb is in the past perfect (*hadn't eaten*) and the second, the later event, in the past simple (*got*): "I hadn't eaten all day yesterday, so I was hungry when I got home." B is in the present, C (printed *earing*, a misprint for *eating*) gives the continuous form, which stresses an activity and is unnatural for a negative state, and D states what was in progress, not an earlier event.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 24. Neither the opposition candidate nor his supporters \_\_\_\_\_\_ convinced about the results of the election.
questions.corrige_markdown:
With *neither ... nor* the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it. The nearer subject is *his supporters* (plural), so the verb is plural: *were*. *Was*, *is* and *has been* are singular, and the sentence is in the past.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
25. We have \_\_\_\_\_\_ milk in the house.

*Options as printed:* A) plenty of   B) many   C) lots of   D) a lot of
questions.corrige_markdown:
*Milk* is an uncountable noun, so *many* (used with countable nouns) is wrong. *Plenty of*, *lots of* and *a lot of* can all be used before an uncountable noun: "We have plenty of / lots of / a lot of milk in the house." Three options are therefore correct and the question has no single key.

**Intended answer: A, C or D (plenty of, lots of, a lot of); B (many) is wrong.**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level English - articles and determiners

questions.enonce_markdown: 26. We were given a/an \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The usual order of adjectives is opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material. Here: *large* (size), *ancient* (age), *round* (shape), *white* (colour), *cotton* (material): "a large ancient round white cotton ball". In B the size adjective is after the material, in C the colour and the material are reversed, and in D the age comes before the size and the colour before the shape.

**Answer: A.**

choix.texte: large ancient round white cotton ball
ancient round white cotton large ball
Large round ancient cotton white ball
Ancient large white round cotton ball

questions.enonce_markdown: 27. Will you be using your car during the weekend? I \_\_\_\_\_\_ borrow it.
questions.corrige_markdown:
A polite, tentative request is made with *I wonder if I could ...* : the present *wonder* with the more polite *could*. A (*can*) is too direct for this request; B mixes a past verb with a present modal, which breaks the sequence of tenses; C (*wondered if I could*) is possible as a still more tentative past form, but the standard form taught for a request made now is D.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 28. Somebody informed you, \_\_\_\_\_\_?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The statement is positive and in the past simple, so the question tag is negative and uses the auxiliary *did*: *didn't*. After *somebody* the pronoun in the tag is *they*. B would need a negative statement, C has the wrong auxiliary and pronoun, and D is in the present.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
29. 'Samah, did you water the garden?' 'Yes, but I \_\_\_\_\_\_ it just. After \_\_\_\_\_\_, it started to rain.'

*Options as printed:* A) needn't have done ...... I had finished   B) needn't do ...... I finished   C) needn't have done ....... I finished   D) needn't do ......... I had finished
questions.corrige_markdown:
*Needn't have done* says that an action was done although it was not necessary: Samah watered the garden and then it rained, so the watering turned out to be unnecessary. *Needn't do* (B and D) refers to the present or the future and does not fit. The choice between A and C is then only between *After I had finished* and *After I finished*, and both are correct after *after* (the past perfect is optional when the order of events is clear). The printed sentence also has a stray *just* after *it*. The key is therefore not certain.

**Intended answer: needn't have done, with After I had finished or After I finished (A or C).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: 30. I wish Maimouna \_\_\_\_\_\_ so critical of me.
questions.corrige_markdown:
After *I wish* about a present situation we use the unreal past, and the verb *to be* takes *were* for all persons in careful English: "I wish Maimouna weren't so critical of me." *Wasn't* is informal, *isn't* is a plain present form, and *won't be* refers to the future.

**Answer: D.**
themes: A Level English - wishes and subjunctive

questions.enonce_markdown: 31. You're late for the workshop. Don't you think it's about time you \_\_\_\_\_\_ preparing for it?
questions.corrige_markdown:
*It's about time* (or *it's high time*) is followed by the past simple with a present or future meaning: "it's about time you started preparing". *Start*, *were starting to* and *can start* do not follow this pattern.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 32. The sentence that is correctly written is \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
A list must be parallel: the items have the same grammatical form. C has three gerunds (reading, swimming, jogging). A mixes gerunds with an infinitive, B has *He like* (no -s) and *red* (for *read*) and mixes forms, and D repeats *to* for the first two verbs but not for the third.

**Answer: C.**

choix.texte: He likes reading, jogging, and to swim
He like to red, swimming, and jog
He likes reading, swimming, and jogging
He likes to read, to swim, and jog

questions.enonce_markdown: 33. You wouldn't have missed the train if you \_\_\_\_\_\_ earlier.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The main clause *wouldn't have missed* is a third conditional (unreal past), so the *if* clause takes the past perfect: *if you had left earlier*. *Left* would belong to a second conditional, and *have left* and *leave* are not possible after *if* here.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
34. The couple hugged \_\_\_\_\_\_ before the event.

*Options as printed:* A) one another   B) themself   C) each other   D) themselves
questions.corrige_markdown:
Two people who hug perform a reciprocal action, so a reciprocal pronoun is needed. The traditional rule uses *each other* for two people and *one another* for more than two, so for *the couple* C is preferred; in modern usage A is also accepted. *Themself* is not standard, and *themselves* is reflexive (each would hug himself or herself), which changes the meaning. Two options (A and C) are acceptable, so the key is not certain.

**Intended answer: C (each other), preferred for two people; A (one another) is also acceptable.**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: 35. *'I am reading a novel,'* is best reported as \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
With a past reporting verb (*told*) the present continuous of direct speech moves back one step to the past continuous: *I am reading* becomes *she was reading*. A keeps the simple present (wrong aspect), B uses the past perfect (which would report *I have read* or *I read*), and D does not shift the tense.

**Answer: C.**

choix.texte: She told me she reads a novel
She told me she had read a novel
She told me she was reading a novel
She told me she is reading a novel

questions.enonce_markdown: 36. I prefer tea \_\_\_\_\_\_ coffee.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The verb *prefer* takes *to* when two things are compared: *prefer X to Y*. *Than* is used with *rather* (I would rather have tea than coffee), and *for* and *instead of* do not follow *prefer* in this pattern.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 37. The statement *'The school gave her an award'* has the \_\_\_\_\_\_ structure.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Subject: *The school*; verb: *gave*; indirect object: *her*; direct object: *an award*. A clause with a verb followed by two objects is S-V-O-O. SVO has only one object, SV has none, and SVOC needs a complement describing the object.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 38. The students are planning a strike action. You \_\_\_\_\_\_ the principal.
questions.corrige_markdown:
*Had better* is followed by the bare infinitive and gives strong advice: "You had better inform the principal." B uses a past participle, C drops *had* (accepted only in casual speech, not in standard written English) and D uses a continuous form that does not give the advice.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
39. The sentence which is correctly punctuated is \_\_\_\_\_\_.

*Options as printed:* A) He asked us, 'Would you like to have dinner with us?'   B) He asked us, Would you like to have dinner with us?   C) He asked us: 'Would you like to have dinner with us'?   D) He asked us, 'Would you like to have dinner with us?'
questions.corrige_markdown:
Direct speech after a reporting verb is introduced by a comma, set between quotation marks, and the question mark belongs inside the quotation marks because the quoted words are the question. B has no quotation marks, and C puts the question mark outside the quotation marks. Options A and D are printed with identical words and punctuation and both are correct, so the question has no single key.

**Intended answer: the sentence printed in A and in D (identical): He asked us, 'Would you like to have dinner with us?'**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level English - spelling and punctuation

questions.enonce_markdown: 40. *'He rushed into the class and shut the door before the teacher could spot him'* is an example of a \_\_\_\_\_\_ sentence.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The sentence has two main clauses joined by *and* (*He rushed into the class* and *(he) shut the door*) and a subordinate clause introduced by *before* (*before the teacher could spot him*). Two or more main clauses plus at least one subordinate clause make a compound-complex sentence.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
**SECTION D: VOCABULARY (10 marks).** Choose the alternative A, B, C, or D that best completes each sentence below.

41. The government has set up a relief \_\_\_\_\_\_ to help victims of the current socio-political crisis.
questions.corrige_markdown:
A *relief fund* is a sum of money collected or set aside to help victims of a disaster or crisis. *Relief collection*, *relief aid* and *relief bank* are not the usual collocation.

**Answer: C.**
themes: A Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown: 42. There's a \_\_\_\_\_\_ on the use of hosepipes because of water shortage.
questions.corrige_markdown:
A *freeze* on something is an official, usually temporary, stop (a freeze on hiring, on prices), which fits a restriction imposed because of a water shortage. A *boycott* is a refusal to buy or take part as a protest, a *taboo* is a ban set by social custom, and a *hesitation* is a pause. The usual word, *ban*, is not offered, so D is the best of the four printed options, with some doubt about B.

**Answer: D.**
themes: A Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown: 43. The principal asked us to dig all the flowers affected by \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown:
*Blight* is a plant disease that makes plants wither, so flowers affected by blight are dug out. *Bight* is a bend of a coast or a loop of rope, *dight* is an archaic word meaning to dress or adorn, and *byte* is a unit of computer data.

**Answer: A.**
themes: A Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown: 44. Mbone cannot write because she has \_\_\_\_\_\_ on her right thumb.
questions.corrige_markdown:
A *whitlow* is a painful infection of the tip of a finger or thumb, which explains why Mbone cannot write. *Wicklow* is the name of an Irish county, and *wiklow* and *weaklow* are not English words.

**Answer: C.**
themes: A Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown: 45. The scientist's findings were deemed \_\_\_\_\_\_ by critics, as they contradicted established theories.
questions.corrige_markdown:
*Unscientific* means not following the principles or methods of science, which is how critics judge findings that contradict established theories. *Non-scientific* only means unrelated to science, *anti-scientific* means hostile to science (an attitude, not a quality of findings) and *pro-scientific* means in favour of science, which does not fit the criticism.

**Answer: A.**
themes: A Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown: 46. While many people advocate for \_\_\_\_\_\_ solution to environmental issues, some argue that immediate action is essential.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The sentence sets a long-term answer against immediate action. A *sustainable* solution is one that can be kept up over time without harming the environment, so people who advocate it are contrasted with those who want action at once. People do not advocate a *superficial*, *extravagant* or *temporary* solution.

**Answer: B.**
themes: A Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown: 47. A \_\_\_\_\_\_ of engineers was dispatched to assess the structural integrity of the Bamenda road project.
questions.corrige_markdown:
A group of people working together on a task is a *team*. A *cluster* is a group of things growing or lying close together, a *bench* is a group of judges or magistrates, and a *troop* is a group of soldiers, scouts or monkeys.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
48. Choose the odd set:

*Options as printed:* A) mango - banana - orange - pineapple   B) honest - brave - courageous - coward   C) run - jog - sprint - dash   D) democracy - monarchy - republic - bureaucracy
questions.corrige_markdown:
A has four fruits and C has four verbs of moving fast, so neither has an odd member. B has an intruder: *coward* is the opposite of *brave* and *courageous*, which are synonyms. D also has an intruder: democracy, monarchy and republic are forms of government, while *bureaucracy* is a system of administration. Both B and D can be defended as the odd set, so the key is not certain.

**Intended answer: B (coward) or D (bureaucracy).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
For question 49, choose the alternative A, B, C, or D which is similar in meaning to the underlined word in this sentence.

49. The author's narrative was **imbued** with a sense of nostalgia that resonated deeply with the audience.
questions.corrige_markdown:
To be *imbued with* a feeling or quality is to be filled or saturated with it. *Lacking* and *removed* mean the opposite, and *simplified* has no relation to the sense.

**Answer: C.**
themes: A Level English - synonyms and antonyms

questions.enonce_markdown:
For question 50, choose the alternative A, B, C, or D that is opposite in meaning to the underlined word in the sentence.

50. Dr. Ngwobela gave a **stellar** presentation on teaching an Argumentative Essay which left everyone impressed.
questions.corrige_markdown:
*Stellar* means outstanding, excellent. The presentation "left everyone impressed", so the opposite is a dull one, *boring*. *Exceptional* is a synonym, not an antonym. *Irrelevant* and *superficial* describe other faults (not relevant, not deep), not the opposite of excellent. The best antonym (*mediocre*) is not offered, so D is the closest.

**Answer: D.**
themes: A Level English - synonyms and antonyms
